A terminal in my pocket: Blink, Tailscale and a computer that never sleeps

Most of my data-science work does not fit into a laptop session. Scrapers run for days, model fits take hours, and a pipeline should not die because I closed a lid. The answer I settled on is boring and works: the long-running jobs live on a computer at home that is always on, and I reach it from everything else through a terminal.

Why the terminal

A terminal is the one interface that works the same on a MacBook, a Linux box and a phone. It is tiny in bandwidth, it survives bad connections, scripts can drive it, and anything I can do in it I can also automate. That is why even the editor, the file manager and the git client I use are terminal apps.

Why a computer that is always on

A job that needs to run for six hours should not depend on my laptop staying awake, charged and online. A cheap desktop in the corner does not care. I start the job, detach, and look at it later from wherever I am. Scraping is the typical case: it is slow by design (be polite to the server), it must not stop halfway, and it does not need my attention while it runs.

Tailscale: one private network

Tailscale puts all my devices on one private network, wherever they physically are. Every machine gets a stable name, there is no port forwarding and nothing is exposed to the internet. My own network has a Mac Studio, a MacBook, two Linux computers, an iPad and an iPhone, and from any of them ssh machine-name just works.

Blink on the iPhone

Blink Shell is a proper terminal for iOS with SSH and Mosh. With Tailscale running on the phone, I can open Blink, connect to the machine at home and attach to the session that is already running. Mosh is the detail that makes it pleasant on mobile: the connection survives switching between Wi-Fi and mobile data and the phone going to sleep.

Typing code on a glass keyboard is the weak spot. For that I use a Clicks keyboard case, which gives the iPhone a physical keyboard with real keys. It is not a laptop replacement, but fixing a path, restarting a job or reading a log from the sofa becomes comfortable.

Everything in one place: tmux and herdr

On every machine the work lives inside a tmux session, so closing the terminal never kills anything. From one terminal I connect to any computer over its Tailscale name and attach to whatever is running there. herdr, the terminal workspace manager I use next to tmux, shows my workspaces and their state in one sidebar, so I see at a glance which session is busy and which agent is waiting for me.

Moving files between machines is a one-liner too: a small just recipe asks which device I mean, lets me pick the file with a fuzzy finder and runs scp. More about that in the post about just.

The checklist

  • A computer that is always on, with sleep disabled and a wired connection if possible.
  • Tailscale on every device, including the phone.
  • tmux for every long job, started on the machine that runs it.
  • A terminal app on the phone (Blink) and, if you type a lot, a physical keyboard.
